title: Long JETS — Iran Deal Jet Fuel Cost Relief
entry: Initiate $26.50-27.50 on Tuesday May 26 open after reviewing Iran overnight news flow. Scale: 70% at Tuesday open, 30% add only if Iran deal formally signed or WTI breaks decisively below $90. Do NOT add above $29 without a confirmed signed agreement — do not chase on rumor.
stop_loss: $24.50 daily close (~9.7% below entry midpoint) — implies WTI surges back above $104 on Iran war escalation, erasing the fuel cost savings thesis
targets: $29.50 — Iran deal signed; WTI drops to $84-88; airlines begin Q2 positive fuel cost pre-announcements, +8.7%
$32.50 — WTI sustained at $78-82; airlines guide Q3 fuel costs 15-20% below budget; summer travel demand beats, +19.8%
$36.00 — Full Hormuz reopening confirmed; WTI to $70-72; airline margin structural reset; consumer gasoline relief boosts travel spend, +32.7%
catalyst: WTI settled at $96.60 on May 22 (CNBC). Trump stated on May 23 that the US-Iran deal is 'largely negotiated' and imminent; Axios published 60-day ceasefire terms on May 24 — Hormuz opens with no tolls, Iran sells oil freely, uranium disposal talks begin. If confirmed and signed, WTI gaps toward $80-85 range. Jet fuel (25-30% of airline operating costs) tracks WTI with a 2-3 week lag. A $15-20/barrel WTI decline saves a major US carrier $800M-$1.2B annually. JETS holds AAL (~10%), UAL (~10%), DAL (~10%), LUV (~7%), and international carriers including Air Canada and Lufthansa.
thesis:
Airlines are the largest industrial buyer of crude oil globally. Jet fuel represents 25-30% of major US airline operating costs, and the Iran war oil shock has cost the US airline industry an estimated $4-6B in annualized excess fuel expenses since WTI broke above $80 in February 2026. JETS has materially underperformed the SPX by 15-20% since the war began — not because of deteriorating demand (summer travel bookings are strong) but because the fuel cost impairment compresses margins and forces capacity reductions that kill earnings leverage. Strip out the war premium and major US carriers were profitable and growing at $70-80 WTI. The Iran deal reverses this from a structural headwind to a structural tailwind in one session.

The Iran deal mechanics favor airlines specifically through three channels: (1) WTI spot falls immediately on a formal signed deal, as Hormuz reopening implies 3.5M barrels/day of Iranian production returning to market within weeks; (2) forward-curve crude (what airlines hedge) collapses simultaneously — if Q3/Q4 2026 WTI forward falls from $94-98 to $78-82, airlines can lock in fuel hedges at those lower levels and guide Q3 fuel costs materially below consensus; (3) US gasoline relief ($4.75/gal today toward $3.40-3.60) directly stimulates the discretionary spending that drives the leisure travel demand driving the June-August peak season. JETS benefits from all three channels within the 2-4 week window. The ETF structure provides additional diversification — a single carrier blowup (labor disruption, mechanical event) doesn't crater the position.

The position is sized small (2%) because the deal is NOT signed as of Memorial Day. Iran's state media (Fars agency) on May 24 called US assertions about Hormuz control 'inconsistent with reality.' This same false-start pattern has appeared three times in the past 90 days, and each prior reversal returned WTI to $100-110. JETS is sized as an asymmetric event bet: a signed deal in the next 1-2 weeks produces 20-33% upside; a confirmed collapse returns the position to pre-deal levels with a controlled 9.7% stop. The $24.50 stop allows the position to absorb one 'false ceasefire' event before the stop triggers, matching the pattern observed in prior deal reversals.
bull_case: Iran-US formal deal signed Tuesday or Wednesday May 26-27. WTI gaps to $83-88; jet fuel forward curve collapses toward $2.40/gallon from $3.10+. AAL, UAL, and DAL issue positive pre-announcements on Q2 fuel cost guidance before June earnings season. Summer 2026 travel bookings strengthen as US gasoline relief boosts consumer confidence. JETS to $32-36 within 3 weeks. Tail: WTI drops to $70-72 by mid-June as Iranian barrels flood the market; airlines guide FY2026 fuel costs 20% below initial budgets; JETS to $38-40, capturing the full blue-sky scenario.
bear_case: Iran state media formally denies the deal framework Tuesday; WTI re-spikes to $103-107 on breakdown signal. Airlines issue Q2 warnings on top-line weakness from summer booking caution. JETS drops to $25.50-26.00. Stop at $24.50 triggered within 3 days. Tail: Iran military action in Hormuz (tanker strike, mine deployment) gaps WTI to $120+ in a single session; JETS drops to $22-23 faster than any stop order can be protected on a gap event. This is the primary reason size is capped at 2% — the tail risk is a single-event gap, not a gradual deterioration.
invalidation: $24.50 daily close, OR WTI back above $105 on confirmed Iran escalation, OR Iranian Foreign Ministry (not just Fars agency) formally denies the deal framework with an official statement

outcome.outcome_label: Thesis broken — Iran attacks Kuwait airport
outcome.note: Iranian drones severely damaged Kuwait International Airport on June 3, killing one person and injuring 63; Iran simultaneously fired ballistic missiles at Bahrain and struck an oil tanker near Kuwait port. The de-escalation thesis is definitively inverted — military action against Gulf-state civilian infrastructure is stronger invalidation than any FM statement. Exiting with a gain before the airspace-closure and fuel-cost-spike effects fully hit JETS.
